title: Captain America: Winter Soldier
author: Ed Brubaker
my_review:
Seeing the details of the Project: Winter Soldier files written in such a brutally detached manner slowly destroyed me. But I expected that.

What I really enjoyed is the less polished "Hollywood" aesthetic and characterisation compared with the MCU. MCU's Steve and Bucky both come across as these pure, good souls that have traversed horrifyingly tragic paths in their lives. This, however, presents a Steve who knows that sometimes methods of questionable morality are the only way forward in war and carries the burden of such sacrifices. And Bucky's job from the beginning was to fight dirty and sneak around in the shadows to stab the enemy in the back.

There are darker edges in the good guys that Hydra are not responsible for. It makes for a more interesting moral battleground, and a more believable war.

title: The Power
author: Naomi Alderman
my_review:
It starts in girls around the age of fourteen. Soon all young girls are born with it. The younger women are able to pass it on to older women who feel like they had it the whole time, but it was hiding somewhere forgotten. All the women of the world quickly learn they have Power - and they're going to use it.

When you read the premise of all women gaining an electrical discharge superpower, you'd be forgiven for thinking it describes a sci-fi or graphic novel. However, The Power is a meticulous piece of literary speculative fiction examining how a small advantage of one gender over the other will over time lead to a gaping chasm of power, authority, respect, expectation, and societal standing between the two sides of the gender binary.

The book is presented as a novel inside a novel - written by a male author in the distant post-Cataclysm future, set in today's time. It follows a small group of characters in the decade after women gain their power, and before the Cataclysm: an apocalyptic event wherein almost all history of the patriarchal societies we know today is wiped out (an event we only know of from the fictional author's writing outside the main narrative).

The book does two things: it shows how there is nothing integral in men or women that leads to the power split, and it explores how the perceived difference in power snowballs through history to build vast inequalities in our society. It does this by introducing a small fantastical element to start the ball rolling in the opposite direction of what we know.

It's an unsettling read. As a female reader it begins as a triumph - seeing the women of the world begin to seize back power. Then there are a few individuals who go too far, but you can reason that they are a minority. It's impossible to detect when the scale of power and privilege tips past equality until you're too deep into the horrors. Until you identify with the male character afraid to walk alone at night - that's a fear you know. Intimately.

The Power is only interested in the gender binary. If you're looking for more nuance in the discussion of gender (or even a mention of a person elsewhere on the gender spectrum) you will be disappointed. It's also a bit lacking in its approach to the uprising of women in the Middle East.

But, ultimately, a fantastic critique of how we allow our modern expectations to corrupt our interpretation of history, and an essential read in a time when women are standing up and speaking out. 4⭐️

title: Artemis
author: Andy Weir
my_review:
I actually burst out laughing at the line in this saying "only an idiot relies on duct tape to maintain a pressure seal." Poor Mark Watney, everyone's favourite sci-fi idiot. First read of 2018, here we go!

Andy Weir's writing appeals very precisely to my kind of nerdery, and like The Martian this was right up my alley. Jazz Bashara is a smuggler in Artemis, the moon's first city, who gets caught up in a heist. Take the formula of every heist movie you love, stage it in a low gravity vacuum, throw in the Weir trademark of pitting the characters up against very probable complications (low-grav vacuum, remember?) and forcing them to "science the shit" past each obstacle, and you have Artemis. I love it.

Straight up, this is not the modern masterpiece that The Martian was. In that book, Mark Watney overcoming all odds on Mars serves the narrative - one man against all the odds (plus the massive global effort of space programs back on Earth). It needs a triumph. So Mark has an uncanny ability to luck (or science) his way out of situations which most certainly should have killed him. In Artemis the story is not of space survival so much as space hijinks. The stakes are still high (again, low-grav vacuum) but that just serves to add tension - it's not the central theme. So when Jazz has the same knack of saving herself from impossible death scenarios, it invites a bit more scepticism.

A couple of miscellaneous good things this book has that I want to praise:

▪️A racially and ethnically diverse cast. Weir has an excellent appreciation of space exploration (and science in general) as a global collaborative effort. He refuses to take the lazy (and inaccurate) route of populating his books with mainly white Americans. In fact, he takes care to detail how Artemis the city couldn't have arisen out of NASA and America.

▪️ A female protagonist - a woman of Muslim heritage no less. I can't speak to the cultural representation but I can talk about the gender. Jazz is exactly the kind of protagonist we need to see more of in our media. Unlike some male authors, the female aspect hasn't been awkwardly stumbled over. Weir has written her as a complete character first (as he would a male character), then upon editing has refined the gendered moments outwith his experience based on female feedback. There are tiny woman-written-by-man moments I as a reader clashed with, but they are few. There's room for improvement but overall we get a well-rounded, three-dimensional female protagonist who is never characterised by, or reduced to, being female. Don't get me wrong, this should be the most basic requirement in writing any character - but it's rare to see. Especially in today's climate where writers are too afraid to do anything other than "stay in their lane", thus saturating our media with white American males. Cause, you know, we needed more of that.

This book is a fantastic space caper, filled with humour, twists and turns, and an abundance of space nerdery. I couldn't be more thankful to live through the birth of this new chapter in sci-fi literature, and I hope to see books like this become more popular. 4⭐️

title: The Hate U Give (The Hate U Give, #1)
author: Angie Thomas
my_review:
"The Hate U Give Little Infants F**ks Everybody".

So I finally got around to reading what a lot of folks in the YA community are calling the book of the year. Angie Thomas has in fact just won the Goodreads awards for Best Young Adult Fiction for The Hate U Give and Debut Goodreads Author. I couldn't agree more.

The greatest joy and the greatest strength of fiction is how it sparks and kindles empathy. Throughout the history of the written word readers have found empathy in some of the most unlikely places. It's the most powerful force of humankind. It allows us to communicate, to forge connections, relationships, to build and foster ideas and tools on a global scale. It unites us, drives the progress of humanity, and we are stronger together.

There are a lot of people and places in the world right now lacking in empathy. The Black Lives Matter movement draws attention to one of them. With social media now allowing underprivileged voices to be heard, what has long been an open secret in black communities is on show for us all.

Racism is alive and thriving. Men, women and children are being preyed upon, assaulted and killed - brutally and remorselessly - by people in the law enforcement system, people who are supposed to protect us all. The victims have their entire history exposed in the media. Is it a lack of education this time? Or is it a petty crime? All symptoms of a society rigged to black people's disadvantage, but that fact is often ignored. These victims are posthumously tried in the court of public opinion, and public opinion is often ruling that these innocent people deserved their own murder! The killers? They walk free, still wearing their badge, still carrying the murder weapon, and we are told the officers are serving the community, protecting the children from these "thugs".

"But what about OUR children?" the black community asks, after witnessing yet another innocent child shot dead by a law enforcement officer. What about the black community? What about the black children? Do their lives not matter? Do black lives not matter?

THUG takes us on a journey with 16 year-old Starr who witnesses the murder of one of these innocent children, her childhood friend, Khalil. As Starr navigates her grief and the greater injustice, both in black and white communities, a deeper understanding unfolds in a white reader like myself. As someone who has never experienced this insurmountable injustice, it is easy to wonder what the individual could have done differently. "Why couldn't they have done this/that? Maybe this wouldn't have happened."

Starr's story introduces you to wisdom from people on different sides of the equation: her ex-convict father, her middle-class police officer uncle, a drug-dealing friend in a gang, her upper-class white boyfriend. In every interaction, in every part of the criminal trial, THUG explains away every question or argument you could possibly have. Even if you are already well-intentioned and have tried to understand, to SEE, THUG takes you gently by the hand and turns you to face the brick wall of injustice black communities live behind. And you can understand better. Hopefully then you can DO better.

It all comes back to empathy. Feeling empathy for our children who have been failed by humanity. Feeling empathy for those who need it most. THUG is a vitally important read for this chapter of history in the western world.

An astounding novel. 5⭐️

title: Da Vinci's Tiger
author: L.M. Elliott
my_review:
This was going to go in an Instagram caption but was way too long:

So many books on my bookshelf and none of them are really inspiring me to read them. Finished this yesterday afternoon and, eh, it's just a bit meh. The voice of the narrative was a bit too childish for me. I managed to persevere and was relieved that the insipid romance I was expecting was nowhere to be found. Instead it was about a sharp young woman and a romance of the intellect, I guess is the best way to put it. It centres on the renaissance era ideal of Platonic love, in which a beautiful woman is held up as the image of virtue to inspire and lead man from his sins. The young heroine (as befitting of her time) sees value in this ideal, yet recognises the constraints and injustices in being held aloft in such a manner, as well as the hypocrisies inherent in such a romanticisation by men of women.


A lot of modern historical fiction for the YA audience often centres on women with absurdly modern feminist ideals which simply could not exist within the fictional setting. It is an annoyance of mine. Yes, it is a good message for younger readers, but I prefer my historical heroines to stay true to their principles in a way that is a truer reflection of the time. A 21st century woman in a 15th century setting is of little value to me. I understand and share her ideals, and of course the discriminatory society seems stupid and unfair to me. But that is only so obvious to me because of centuries and centuries of women pushing their boundaries bit by bit, collectively making my life begin closer to even-footing than theirs could ever have been. Were I actually born in a historical setting, these injustices would just be irrevocable facts of life. What inspires me in historical fiction is reading about women finding strength and grace in their positions which are so unfair and confined to my modern mindset. I wonder at how they could live such a life, yet they find small ways to rattle their cage bars, improve themselves and make the world just that little bit more fair. That is inspiring to me.


Here, for example, Ginevra accepts her role as muse and Platonic lover for the sake of being able to challenge the conventions of female portraiture. Sitting pretty for a picture, how unfeminist for today's standards! And yet her portrait becomes one of the first in which a woman looks directly at the viewer, daring him to look into her eyes and see there is intelligence behind them, that she is not something passive simply to be gazed upon. She also spends a great deal of her time in a nunnery. How quaint and backwards! A woman having to pray regularly to maintain a facade of virtue. And yet, the abbess at this nunnery encourages the novices to read the great minds of the time. In fact, freed from their roles as bargaining chips in arranged marriages, these women have the freedom to educate themselves. The ways in which women have tried to liberate themselves, big and small, are what makes female-centred historical fiction inspiring to me.


So yeah, I managed to get into a big rant, yet I still didn't particularly care for this book. 😅 Ginevra was authentic in the way I described above but very naive, occasionally unbearably so. It gets points for having substance and some authenticity, but not the most enjoyable read.
